public_comment.topic: Asked whether public comment on each budget section can be made now or must wait for next week's formal public hearing.

Criticized the town manager's proposal to cut the grant writer/manager position and use $50,000 for a pavement pilot instead, and questioned cemetery- and pavement-related capital requests as lacking a plan.
Explained how a Worcester Regional Retirement COLA would translate into a small monthly pension increase, and noted the impact of health-insurance costs on retirees on fixed incomes.
Urged the committee to scrutinize the core school budget itself (teacher cuts, salary lines, transportation increases), separate from the override question.
Suggested putting a QR code or link on the printed Finance Committee report so voters can access more information before town meeting.
Explained the financial-approval language in the cemetery citizen petition article and proposed spending $50,000 on cemetery electrical/lighting instead of pavement crack-sealing.
Listed a range of unresolved town financial pressures (storm water utility, sewer commission default rate, PFAS remediation costs, trash pickup funding) for the committee to weigh.

budget_items.what_was_said: The overlay reserve was originally budgeted at $250,000 but has been reduced by the assessors to $175,000.
A transfer of certified free cash to the Lunenburg Public Schools' FY26 operating budget was proposed as a stop-gap ahead of a possible FY27 override.
The planned $100,000 transfer to the general stabilization account was reduced to zero to help fund the school transfer.
The planned transfer to special-purpose stabilization funds was eliminated entirely.
Three special projects were proposed totaling $152,500: TCP decommissioning, an assessors' DOR directive, and Cemetery Road network repairs.
FY25 transfers total $465,000 in the warrant, though the snow-and-ice deficit portion may come in below the printed figure.
An additional $50,000 was requested to cover unanticipated special-education student move-ins in FY25, on top of $150,000 already absorbed.
A $36,250 grant reimbursement transfer was removed pending research into whether it must be repaid.
The FY26 capital program totals $655,000, partly funded by shifting unused FY23 capital funds.
A new one-time $10,000 fund was proposed to cover payouts for employees separating from service.
After all proposed FY26 appropriations, free cash would fall from about $2.2 million currently certified to roughly $219,524.
The consolidated FY26 general government budget, now including several relocated departments, totals about $2,962,263.
Legal expenses were increased $10,000 despite what officials called a favorable flat-fee contract.
The unfilled $50,000 grant manager/writer position was proposed for elimination to help restore pavement management; a member pushed back and floated a free-cash-funded pilot instead.
The FinCom reserve fund line was reduced from $200,000 toward $185,000 for FY26, called still a healthy level.
A $210,000 salary reserve fund was proposed to cover upcoming police and DPW/Teamsters bargaining increases and non-union COLAs.
The proposed non-union COLA was raised from 2.5% to 3% (about $7,000 more) after pushback, well short of the roughly $40,000 cost of matching the clerical union's 5%.
IT/communications staff hours were made permanent at an increased level, adding $14,800.
IT department expenses overall increased by $166,000.
The internal network IT administrator position was eliminated, a $79,000 salary decrease, as support shifts further to an outsourced contractor.
The outsourced IT contract line grew from a $25,000 (revised $66,203) budget to a new $159,285 contract for FY26, partly offset by ARPA funds only this current year.
The FY26 police budget totals about $2,434,772; it appears reduced only because negotiated raises sit in the salary reserve, not the department line.
The police motorcycle lease, expiring in October and already paid through then, was eliminated to help fund pavement management.
The FY26 fire budget totals about $1,744,588 and excludes a proposed fourth shift/42-hour work week expected as an FY27 override item.
A new benefit allowing holiday pay for call firefighters was estimated to cost up to about $7,000.
The consolidated 'other protection' category totals $368,900; regional dispatch stayed flat after Hudson joined the agreement.

Several school budget totals were given, including a town-manager-recommended figure, a prior override amount, a special town meeting transfer, and a net increase described as $94,900 (3.64%); captions rendered these inconsistently.
The Monty Tech assessment was described as rising substantially, with the percentage and dollar amount rendered inconsistently.
The FY26 DPW budget totals about $2,476,195, not reflecting still-unresolved union salary adjustments.
Pavement management, once cut to zero, was restored to $279,000 rather than the prior $550,000 target.
Chapter 90 state road aid is expected near $69,900 (later given as $69,700), down from about $418,000 the prior year, pending a state bond bill.
Facilities totals about $1,673,196, including roughly $155,000 more in utilities/maintenance and a $27,000 internal offset for lost TCP rental revenue as schools vacate.
The Council on Aging budget rises $31,500 as formula grants move into the operating budget, plus $33,000 more for programs, while a 10-hour outreach position is eliminated by mutual agreement.
The veteran services (Chapter 115) benefits line was reduced, said to still leave room for new qualifying residents; the figure was truncated in captions.
The new culture-and-recreation category totals about $639,036.70 and funds 100 extra floating library-director hours but not a proposed $18,000/year teen-room position.
Debt service decreases $393,100; total FY26 principal and interest is about $2.5 million across excluded and non-excluded debt.
Now folded into the omnibus budget, the retirement assessment rises $264,700 (12.4%) to about $2,392,572, partly from a state-mandated retiree COLA repaid over years.
Although the actual increase is 14.84%, the town-side line rises only about 7%, using a previously built-in budget cushion.
The line was built from actuals plus 14.84% and an estimate of five additional family plans, flagged as needing closer tracking for FY27.
The number of employees, including school, on town health plans ranged from about 531 to 540 month to month.
The FY26 sewer enterprise budget totals about $1,886,152.
Proposed transfers include $19,124 to a sewer stabilization fund and a smaller amount to a sewer reserve capacity stabilization fund.
Pay-as-you-throw revenue of $500,000 funds trash, with total trash-and-recycling costs (including tax-supported recycling) around $1 million; a comparison town subsidizes recycling far less.
A $45,000 item appears under the water enterprise budget.
Declining cable-provider revenue means the PEG (public access) program is drawing down its own retained earnings to stay funded.
A citizen filed an override petition equal to the gap between the school committee's approved (cut) budget and its level-service budget, meant to let voters restore school cuts directly.
A committee member questioned how much of the school increase is attributable to special education/out-of-district tuition, citing inconsistent public figures.
The DPW director position was proposed to be regraded from A16 to A17 for competitive-salary alignment.
A $22,500 transfer to the OPEB trust fund was proposed per town financial policy.
A previously voted $300,000 TCP roof repair may need to be re-voted because the original vote specified a location on the portion of the building now slated to close.
A roughly $100,000 school-requested article to fix a bulging wall and drainage has no identified funding source and may be withdrawn or passed over.
A pending reserve-fund transfer request from the fire chief for vehicle maintenance, roughly $10,000-11,000, awaits committee action.

minutes.headline: FinCom reviewed the full FY26 town/school budget and a ~$2M citizen override petition for schools; no votes taken.
minutes.summary: The Finance Committee heard the Town Manager's complete FY26 budget presentation department by department, including a restructured chart of accounts, a proposed $500,000 free-cash transfer to the schools, restored pavement funding, and a 14.84% health insurance increase. It also heard a citizen's Proposition 2½ override petition (roughly $2 million) to restore school cuts, and a member's presentation finding unreconciled figures in the school budget, prompting agreed-upon follow-up data requests. No substantive votes were taken; the board plans to vote on all warrant articles and finalize its annual report the following week.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee reviewed the full FY26 town and school budget department by department, but took no votes.
A citizen-petitioned Proposition 2½ override to restore school cuts was presented and discussed, with a vote deferred to next week.
A committee member's independent review found unreconciled figures in the school budget, prompting agreed follow-up data requests.
The committee planned a free-cash transfer to schools as a stop-gap toward a possible FY27 override, while cutting planned stabilization transfers.
The committee set a backup meeting for April 7 to finalize its annual report ahead of the print deadline.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on the full FY26 town and school budget and the override petition at town meeting next week.
An unreconciled school budget could still change the figures printed in the committee's annual report before that vote.
Using free cash and cutting planned stabilization transfers to cover schools this year shifts money from savings toward current spending.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree on most budget figures and differ mainly in what each chose to record. The official minutes record the deferred override vote and the option 1 decision, which ours miss, while ours record data requests, filing and scheduling decisions the official minutes omit. A reader should check the override vote, who sat as Vice Chair and whether Tom Gray was present, and the figures that differ beyond digit errors (Facilities, free cash, capital program).
